candidate_sources.title: Alternaria triticina (leaf blight of wheat)
candidate_sources.snippet: Infection is first evident as small, oval, discoloured lesions, irregularly scattered on the leaves. As the lesions enlarge they become dark-brown to grey and irregular in shape. Some are surrounded by a bright-yellow marginal zone. Infection usually starts on the lower leaves. Conidia germinate in temperatures between 20–25°C. Yield losses reaching 60%.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria Leaf Blight | Pests & Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: The disease causes necrotic leaf lesions and in severe cases shriveling of the leaves. Infection will only occur on hosts older than three weeks with symptoms appearing at 7–8 weeks of age. Foliar fungicides such as mancozeb, ziram, copper oxychloride, and propineb can prevent further infection.

candidate_sources.title: WHEAT :: MAJOR DISEASES :: LEAF BLIGHT
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed description of wheat leaf blight caused by Alternaria triticina including symptoms on leaves, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and management recommendations for Indian wheat-growing conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial leaf streak and black chaff on small grains
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf streak (BLS) is a disease of wheat, barley, triticale, oats and many other grasses caused by Xanthomonas translucens. BLS infection initially becomes present as water-soaked lesions on leaves, with advanced infections developing black chaff symptoms on glumes. Streaks turn yellow then brown, reducing photosynthetic potential of the flag leaf.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Streak and Black Chaff of Wheat | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf streak and black chaff of wheat caused by Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa. Covers symptoms on leaves (water-soaked streaks turning brown) and heads (dark purple to black streaks on glumes), disease cycle, conditions favoring disease, and management including certified seed and resistant varieties. Yield losses up to 40 percent reported.

candidate_sources.title: Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa (bacterial leaf streak of wheat and barley) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet for Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa covering identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, detection, management and economic impact of bacterial leaf streak on wheat and barley.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Streak and Black Chaff of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf streak and black chaff are caused by Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa. Early leaf infections are characterized by irregular translucent water-soaked streaks. Streaks eventually turn yellow and then brown, reducing photosynthetic potential. Severe head symptoms are called black chaff with distinct thin black streaks on glumes and lemmas. Yield losses range from negligible to greater than 50%.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Barley yellow dwarf (BYD) is the most widely distributed and economically important viral disease of wheat. Caused by barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV) and cereal yellow dwarf virus (CYDV), transmitted by aphids. Symptoms include yellowing, reddening, or purpling of leaf tips and margins, stunting, reduced tillering, and decreased yields up to 20%.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf of Wheat, Oats, and Barley - Ohioline (Ohio State University)
candidate_sources.snippet: Factsheet on barley yellow dwarf disease of cereals. Covers symptoms (yellow, red, or purple discoloration of flag leaves from tip down), pathogen biology (Luteoviridae family viruses BYDV-PAV, BYDV-MAV, CYDV-RPV), aphid vectors (bird cherry-oat aphid, English grain aphid, corn leaf aphid, greenbug), and management including delayed planting and resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf | CropWatch | University of Nebraska-Lincoln
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed guide on barley yellow dwarf in wheat. Symptoms include yellow, red, or purple leaf discoloration from tip to base and margin to midrib, stunted plants with shortened internodes. Caused by BYDV and CYDV, transmitted by over 20 aphid species. Management includes delayed fall planting, insecticidal seed treatments (neonicotinoids), and tolerant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Cephalosporium Stripe of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Cephalosporium stripe, caused by the soilborne fungus Cephalosporium gramineum (sexual stage: Hymenula cerealis), is the only known vascular wilt disease of small grain cereals. Yellow (chlorotic) stripes in leaves running from tip to base are characteristic. Disease control relies on cultural practices and variety selection.

candidate_sources.title: Cephalosporium Stripe | Wheat & Small Grains | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellow stripes running from the tip of the leaf blade to its base and down the leaf sheath is characteristic of Cephalosporium stripe. The soilborne fungus Cephalosporium gramineum overwinters in infected crop residue. Plants are infected through root wounds caused by cultivation, frost heaving, freeze damage, or soil insects. Liming to raise soil pH is effective in controlling the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Cephalosporium Stripe | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Cause: The fungus Cephalosporium gramineum (teleomorph Hymenula cerealis), a soilborne organism that survives in crop residue. Symptoms include one to three yellow stripes per leaf connected to darkened veins. Infection favored by cool (45-55°F) and moist conditions. Seed treatments and foliar fungicides are not effective; control relies on crop rotation, soil pH management, and variety selection.

candidate_sources.title: Common Bunt of Wheat | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Common bunt is caused by two fungal species, Tilletia caries and Tilletia laevis. Wheat grains are replaced by brown-black bunt balls that produce an unpleasant fishy smell (trimethylamine), hence the name stinking smut. Head symptoms begin to appear during flowering, with spikelets that may appear off-green and greasy as heads ripen. Favored when infected seed is planted into cool, moist soil.

candidate_sources.title: Stinking Smut (Common Bunt) of Wheat | APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Tilletia caries (synonymous with Tilletia tritici) is a basidiomycete that causes common bunt or stinking smut of wheat, a historically devastating disease that has reemerged in organic wheat agriculture. Infected ovaries appear greasy with a dark green cast; when squeezed they reveal a mass of black spores that smell like rotting fish (trimethylamine). Bunt balls develop into hardened masses resembling miniature footballs.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) - Common Bunt (Stinking Smut) | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Common bunt (stinking smut) of wheat caused by Tilletia caries and Tilletia laevis. Covers symptoms, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and chemical and cultural management recommendations for Pacific Northwest wheat production. Infected kernels replaced by bunt balls filled with dark spore masses with characteristic foul odor.

candidate_sources.title: Dwarf Bunt of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Dwarf bunt caused by Tilletia controversa affects winter wheat. Symptoms include 50% reduction in plant height, excessive tillering, yellow leaf flecking, and bunt balls filled with dark spores having a fishy odor. Spores germinate at 0-8°C under snow cover.

candidate_sources.title: Tilletia controversa (dwarf bunt of wheat) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet on Tilletia controversa, causal agent of dwarf bunt of wheat. Covers identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, and management including resistant varieties and seed treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Dwarf Bunt | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Cause: Tilletia controversa, a fungus carried on seed that survives many years in soil. Grows optimally at 37-46°F under snow cover, infects seedlings after emergence at 2-5 leaf stage. Management includes resistant varieties and seed treatment with Dividend Extreme.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot of wheat, also known as strawbreaker foot rot, is caused by Oculimacula yallundae and Oculimacula acuformis. Infection results in characteristic elliptical or eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem with a dark brown perimeter. The center of each lesion is typically yellowish-brown. Eyespot lesions weaken the stem, which may result in multidirectional lodging.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot of Wheat: How to identify and control this common fungal disease | OSU Extension Service
candidate_sources.snippet: OSU Extension factsheet on eyespot of wheat caused by Oculimacula yallundae and O. acuformis. Covers identification of eye-shaped lesions on lower stems, disease cycle favored by cool moist conditions (45-55°F), survival on infected straw residue, and control measures including resistant varieties with Pch1 and Pch2 genes.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot | Wheat & Small Grains | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: WSU guide on eyespot (strawbreaker foot rot) of wheat. Describes symptoms as diffuse elliptical lesions on leaf sheaths near soil surface, yellow-brown lesions with dark scurf in center. Fungus colonizes successive leaf sheaths and true stem, destroying structural and conducting tissues, causing lodging or whiteheads. Management includes Pch1 and Pch2 resistance genes and fungicide application between tillering and second node stage.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root, Crown, and Foot Rot of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium root, crown, and foot rot is caused by several Fusarium spp. Symptoms include dark brown lesions on primary and secondary roots, with a dark brown to red lesion apparent near the first node of the wheat plant. Pink, cottony fungal growth may be evident inside lower portions of infected stems, and infected plants may die prematurely, resulting in white heads.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Fusarium Root, Crown, and Foot Rot (Crown Rot, Foot Rot, Seedling Blight, Dryland Foot Rot) | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium crown rot, also called dryland foot rot, dryland root rot, and Fusarium root rot. Several Fusarium species including F. culmorum and F. pseudograminearum infect roots and crowns of spring and winter wheat. Roots are brown, subcrown internode is discolored. After heading, white heads may develop that may be void of kernels or produce shriveled kernels.

candidate_sources.title: Diagnostic Guide: Fusarium Crown Rot of Winter Wheat | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide for Fusarium crown rot of winter wheat. Provides detailed diagnostic criteria, symptoms, and management recommendations for this disease caused by Fusarium pseudograminearum and F. culmorum.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Nodorum Blotch a.k.a. Septoria Glume Blotch | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria nodorum blotch (also known as glume blotch) is caused by the fungus Parastagonospora nodorum (syn. Stagonospora nodorum, Septoria nodorum). Symptoms include grey/brown/purple lesions on glumes and small yellow spots on lower leaves that enlarge into gray or brown elliptical lesions with chlorotic margins. Yield losses of 10-20% when both leaves and heads are damaged; grain is often small and shriveled.

candidate_sources.title: Stagonospora Leaf and Glume Blotch of Wheat | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch is caused by Parastagonospora nodorum. On foliage, symptoms begin as small yellow flecks developing into lens-shaped lesions with yellow halos. On heads, purple-brown or grayish brown streaks start at glume tips and spread throughout the spike. Can cause up to 50% yield loss. Management includes crop rotation, resistant varieties, residue management, and fungicide application at Feekes 8-10.5.1.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria nodorum blotch of wheat | APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: APS plant disease lesson on Septoria nodorum blotch of wheat caused by Parastagonospora nodorum (syn. Phaeosphaeria nodorum, Stagonospora nodorum). Covers disease cycle, symptoms on leaves and glumes, environmental conditions favoring disease (moderate temperatures 68-75°F, wet rainy weather), and integrated management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight or Head Scab of Wheat, Barley and other Small Grain Crops | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium head blight (FHB) or head scab caused by Fusarium graminearum. Earliest symptom occurs soon after flowering with diseased spikelets turning light-straw colored and bleached. Pink or salmon-colored spores on spikelets. Infected kernels called tombstones due to shriveled chalky appearance. Mycotoxin vomitoxin (DON) accumulates in grain.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight (Scab) of Small Grains | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension publication covering Fusarium head blight (scab) of small grains including wheat and barley. Caused by Fusarium graminearum. Covers symptoms, disease cycle, environmental conditions favoring infection (48-72 hours moisture, 75-85°F), and integrated management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight of Wheat | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry on Fusarium head blight of wheat. FHB caused by Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae). Covers symptoms including premature bleaching of spikelets, tombstone kernels, DON mycotoxin contamination. Management via resistant cultivars, fungicides, crop rotation, and tillage practices. Yield losses 10-70%.

candidate_sources.title: Karnal Bunt | Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
candidate_sources.snippet: Karnal bunt, caused by the fungus Tilletia indica, is a disease of wheat, durum wheat, and triticale. APHIS regulates this disease because many trading partners require U.S. wheat be certified as grown in areas free of Karnal bunt. Quarantined to portions of two counties in Arizona with minimal incidence.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Karnal Bunt (Partial Bunt) | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Karnal bunt (partial bunt) caused by Tilletia indica. Symptoms include blackened kernels with fishy odor (trimethylamine), canoe-shaped hollowed kernels. Disease favors cool humid conditions at heading. Management includes resistant varieties and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Tilletia indica (Karnal bunt of wheat) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet on Tilletia indica covering identity, distribution, biology, ecology, hosts, symptoms, prevention and control. T. indica invades kernels and obtains nutrients from the endosperm, leaving waste products with disagreeable odor making bunted kernels unpalatable for flour or pasta.

candidate_sources.title: Loose Smut of Wheat — Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Loose smut of wheat is caused by the fungus Ustilago tritici. Diseased heads consist of olive-black masses of teliospores in place of kernels. The smut spores are enclosed in a fragile, gray membrane that soon ruptures to release airborne spores. Affected plants head out early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels.

candidate_sources.title: Loose Smut / Small Grains / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Loose smut caused by Ustilago tritici. Infection remains invisible until head emergence. Diseased heads contain olive-brown smut spores in place of grain. Management includes systemic fungicide seed treatments, certified seed, and resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Smut Disease in wheat: Tilletia tritici; Ustilago tritici — CABI Plantwise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet covering smut diseases in wheat including loose smut (Ustilago tritici) and common bunt (Tilletia tritici). Covers symptoms, pathogen biology, distribution, management, and prevention measures.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew of Wheat | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Powdery mildew of wheat caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Symptoms include white to gray cottony fungal growth on upper leaf surface. Pathogen reduces photosynthesis and increases respiration and transpiration rates. Cleistothecia develop as plants mature.

candidate_sources.title: Identification and Control of Powdery Mildew of Wheat in Georgia | UGA Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension publication covering identification, symptoms, disease cycle, and control of powdery mildew of wheat caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Includes management strategies including resistant cultivars and fungicide application.

candidate_sources.title: Blumeria graminis (powdery mildew of grasses and cereals) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet on Blumeria graminis, the causal agent of powdery mildew of grasses and cereals including wheat. Covers taxonomy, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, and management of the pathogen.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Root Rot of Wheat | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium root rot of wheat is caused by Pythium spp. (syn. Globisporangium spp.), fungus-like microorganisms that live for years in soil and on old root debris. Symptoms include stunting, yellowing, tiller reduction, and poor stand. Infected roots are shorter, have few root hairs, and are necrotic. Cool, wet, poorly-drained soils favor disease. Seed treatments with metalaxyl or mefenoxam provide limited early protection.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Pythium Root Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium spp. (syn. Globisporangium spp.) are fungus-like microorganisms that parasitize wheat roots. Mild infections reduce population and tillering, delay maturation. Adult plants may be stunted and chlorotic, as if nitrogen deficient. Heads may contain shriveled grain. Symptoms are often uniform across the field and difficult to recognize. Severe infections cause general root rot with loss of cortex (rat-tail appearance).

candidate_sources.title: Disease Caused by Pythium | Penn State Plant Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: After Pythium colonizes roots it causes extensive damage to the root system. Symptoms include lack of small feeder roots, brown lesions, and loss of cortex (rat tail like appearance with central vascular tissue remaining while outer cortex cells fall away). Pythium causes damping-off, seedling blight, and root rot across many crops including wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizoctonia Root Rot of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia root rot (bare patch) is caused by Rhizoctonia solani and R. oryzae. Field symptoms include bare patches or areas of uneven plant height. Severe infection causes plants to be stunted, appear drought stressed or nutrient deprived. The pathogen prunes roots by girdling them, reducing root mass. Roots develop characteristically fine, sharp-looking, red-brown points known as spear tip. Management includes destroying grassy weeds and volunteer hosts (green bridge), minimum 2-3 week interval before seeding, and fungicide seed treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Small Grain Root and Crown Diseases - MSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Montana State University Extension factsheet covering small grain root and crown diseases including Rhizoctonia root rot and damping-off. Damping off is caused by Pythium spp., Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia spp., and Cochliobolus spp. It is soil borne and has increased with no-till management due to cooler, wetter soils in the spring. Symptoms generally occur in circular patches with stunted, yellow plants that may be mistaken for nitrogen deficiency.

candidate_sources.title: Economic Loss from Rhizoctonia Bare Patch in Rainfed Winter Wheat and Spring Barley in Oregon | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: APS publication documenting economic loss from Rhizoctonia bare patch (caused by Rhizoctonia solani AG-8) in rainfed winter wheat and spring barley in Oregon. Rhizoctonia bare patch causes circular patches of stunted or dead plants in wheat fields, with characteristic spear-tipped roots and reduced root systems.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria tritici Blotch of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria tritici blotch is a common disease of wheat caused by Zymoseptoria tritici. Elliptical, tan-brown lesions with yellowish halos appear on seedling leaves, with dark fruiting bodies giving the lesion a characteristic speckled appearance. Subsequent lesions follow leaf veins with straight edges. An integrated approach incorporating variety selection, cultural practices, crop rotation and fungicides is recommended.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf Blotch Diseases of Wheat—Septoria tritici Blotch, Stagonospora nodorum Blotch and Tan Spot | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria tritici blotch, Stagonospora nodorum blotch and tan spot are the three most frequently occurring leaf blotch diseases of wheat. Caused by Zymoseptoria tritici (previously Mycosphaerella graminicola). Diagnostic feature is the presence of black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) within the blotches giving a speckled appearance. Can cause 20-30% yield losses in wet years.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria tritici blotch (STB) of wheat - APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive disease lesson on Septoria tritici blotch caused by Zymoseptoria tritici. Covers symptoms, disease cycle, pathogen biology, epidemiology, and management including resistant cultivars and fungicide resistance concerns. The rapid evolution of pathogen resistance to fungicides is a major barrier.

candidate_sources.title: Sharp eyespot symptoms in cereals | AHDB
candidate_sources.snippet: Sharp eyespot is caused by Rhizoctonia cerealis (Ceratobasidium cereale). Symptoms are elongated, eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem bordered by a dark brown edge that sharply delineates infected area from surrounding tissue. Centers often covered with white fungal growth. The fungus overwinters as mycelium on infected stubble and sclerotia. Cool temperatures around 9°C associated with earlier infection and more severe disease.

candidate_sources.title: The escalating threat of Rhizoctonia cerealis, the causal agent of sharp eyespot in wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of sharp eyespot caused by Rhizoctonia cerealis. Disease has become endemic in many countries and is an escalating threat to world wheat production. Covers symptoms (elliptical stem-base lesions with dark brown perimeter), pathogen biology, yield impact (up to 25% loss in severe cases), resistance genetics (Pch1, Pch2 genes), and management strategies including resistant varieties and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Barley (Hordeum vulgare)-Sharp Eyespot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: PNW Pest Management Handbook entry for sharp eyespot caused by Rhizoctonia cerealis (Ceratobasidium cereale). Covers the same pathogen affecting wheat and barley. Includes disease identification, symptoms on stem base, pathogen biology, and management recommendations including minimal tillage, crop rotation to legumes or spring cereals for 3+ years, and resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat stem rust - Cereal Disease Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat stem rust caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. Uredinia appear as oval lesions on leaf sheaths, true stem, and spike. Dark orange to brick-red raised powdery pustules with ragged edges. Losses often severe (50-70%) over large areas.

candidate_sources.title: Stem Rust of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Stem rust of wheat caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. Comprehensive encyclopedia entry covering symptoms, disease cycle, pathogen biology, and management recommendations for stem rust in wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Rust Diseases of Wheat - Nebraska Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering rust diseases of wheat including stem rust, leaf rust, and stripe rust. Details symptoms, environmental conditions favoring disease, and fungicide management options.

candidate_sources.title: Stripe Rust (Yellow Rust) of Wheat | CAES Field Report
candidate_sources.snippet: Stripe rust, or yellow rust, is primarily a foliar fungal disease of wheat caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. Appears as yellow to orange urediniospores erupting from pustules arranged in long, narrow stripes on leaves between veins, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns. Optimum infection at 50-60°F. Management includes resistant varieties and fungicide application.

candidate_sources.title: An Overview of Stripe Rust of Wheat - Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive overview of stripe rust of wheat caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. Covers symptoms, disease cycle, environmental conditions favoring development (cool temperatures, intermittent rain or dew), and management strategies including resistant varieties and fungicide timing.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Stripe Rust - USDA ARS Cereal Disease Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: USDA Agricultural Research Service Cereal Disease Laboratory page on wheat stripe rust (yellow rust) caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. Covers pathogen biology, race identification, disease monitoring, and resistance breeding. Authoritative federal source for cereal rust surveillance.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Take-All | MU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Take-all is caused by the fungus Gaeumannomyces graminis. Symptoms are most obvious near heading, when plants appear uneven in height, begin to die prematurely, and exhibit white heads. Plants affected by Take-all have darkened stem bases and black, brittle roots.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Take-all | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Cause: Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici. Symptoms include reduced tillering, lack of heading, bleached or empty heads, shriveled kernels, bleached plants dying prematurely, rotting roots, crown and basal culm tissue with shiny dark-brown to black surface mat of fungal tissue beneath the leaf sheath at the base of the plants.

candidate_sources.title: Root Rots on Wheat | Oklahoma State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Take-all caused by Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici. The stem base is covered with a coal-black fungal growth under leaf sheaths. Individual roots turn coal black. Plants are stunted, mature early, and have white empty heads.

candidate_sources.title: Tan Spot of Wheat – Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Tan spot is caused by Pyrenophora tritici-repentis. Initial symptoms are small brown spots on leaves that enlarge into tan necrotic lesions with a yellow halo and diamond-shaped appearance. Covers disease cycle, symptoms, scouting, and management including crop rotation, resistant varieties, and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Fungal Leaf Spot Diseases of Wheat: Tan spot, Septoria/Stagonospora nodorum blotch and Septoria tritici blotch – NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: NDSU extension publication covering tan spot alongside Septoria tritici blotch and Stagonospora nodorum blotch. Describes tan spot symptoms as oval to diamond-shaped tan lesions with yellow halos and dark centers, caused by Pyrenophora tritici-repentis. Includes pathogen biology, disease cycle, and integrated management.

candidate_sources.title: Tan Spot – CropWatch – University of Nebraska-Lincoln
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska extension resource on tan spot of wheat caused by Pyrenophora tritici-repentis (anamorph Drechslera tritici-repentis). Describes symptoms including small brown lesions expanding to tan diamond-shaped spots with yellow borders and dark eyespot centers. Covers disease favoring conditions, survival on wheat stubble, and management through rotation, tillage, resistant varieties, and fungicide application.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat leaf rust - USDA Cereal Disease Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat leaf rust caused by Puccinia triticina. Comprehensive information on biology, epidemiology, and management of leaf rust from the USDA-ARS Cereal Disease Laboratory in St. Paul, MN. Covers race surveys, resistance genes, and disease cycle.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) - Leaf Rust (Brown Rust) | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf Rust (Brown Rust) caused by Puccinia triticina. Symptoms include round to oblong brick-red pustules (uredinia) on leaves. Development favored by mild days 20-25°C with adequate moisture for nighttime dew. Management includes resistant varieties and fungicide application.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaves of infected plants show a yellowed mosaic pattern of parallel discontinuous streaks. WSMV is transmitted by the wheat curl mite (Aceria tosichella). Plants are stunted, may be splayed on the ground, and do not tiller as well as unaffected plants. Cultural practices including volunteer wheat destruction and planting date management are key.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus - Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is transmitted by the wheat curl mite. Symptoms include light green to yellow mottled mosaic streaks parallel to leaf veins. Management focuses on eliminating volunteer wheat (green bridge), adjusting planting dates, and using resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus and the Wheat Curl Mite | University of Kentucky Entomology
candidate_sources.snippet: The wheat curl mite (Aceria tosichella) vectors wheat streak mosaic virus. Symptoms include yellow mosaic on leaves, plant stunting, decreased grain yield, and plant death. Cultural practices are the best means for managing the wheat curl mite and WSMV, including destruction of volunteer wheat at least 2 weeks prior to planting.
